Adult Twospot surgeonfish (Ctenochaetus binotatus) attain a maximum total length of 22 centimeters [Li = 22 centimeters], a measurement consistent with the moderate body sizes observed among members of the genus Ctenochaetus. This ultimate length is typically reached after several years of sustained somatic growth on shallow coral reefs, where the species grazes upon fine algal turfs. Field surveys in the Indo-Pacific indicate that sexually mature individuals frequently exceed 15 centimeters in total length, with the asymptote of 22 centimeters [Li = 22 centimeters] confirming the species' moderate body size among its congeners. The morphological transition from juvenile to adult body plan occurs well before this maximum size is attained, with the onset of reproductive capability marked by a distinct pubertal threshold. In comparison to the congener Zebrasoma scopas, which reaches approximately 40 centimeters, Ctenochaetus binotatus occupies a smaller adult size range, a trait that likely influences its foraging ecology and vulnerability to predation. The species exhibits a typical acanthurid body profile, with a compressed laterally deep form that facilitates maneuverability within complex reef structures. Maximum recorded lengths provide a foundation for understanding growth trajectories and population demographic structure.

Sexual maturation in Ctenochaetus binotatus commences once individuals achieve a total length of approximately 7.3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 7.3 centimeters], a size corresponding to the pubertal transition. This length at puberty (7.3 centimeters) [Lp = 7.3 centimeters] was inferred by scaling from the relative size at maturation documented in the larger congener Zebrasoma scopas, which initiates reproduction at roughly 13.2 centimeters given its ultimate length of 40 centimeters. At this developmental milestone, the gonads become functionally active, enabling individuals to participate in spawning aggregations typical of many acanthurid fishes. The body mass associated with the pubertal transition is estimated at approximately 11 grams [Wwp = approximately 11 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship parameters established for the species. This modest pubertal weight reflects the relatively small body size at which Ctenochaetus binotatus begins its reproductive career, a strategy that may confer advantages in terms of early reproductive output despite the trade-offs inherent in allocating resources to somatic growth versus gamete production. Individuals below this size threshold are reproductively inactive and primarily focused on foraging and predator avoidance within the reef matrix.

Under the stable thermal conditions characteristic of tropical coral reef environments, maintained at 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], female Twospot surgeonfish exhibit a remarkable reproductive capacity. Each mature female may release a single clutch containing approximately 685 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 685 eggs per spawning event], and field observations indicate that such spawning events occur once per day throughout the peak breeding season [F_R_i = events occur once per day throughout the peak breeding season]. This high-frequency reproductive strategy, while energetically demanding, allows for the continuous production of pelagic larvae that may exploit ephemeral planktonic food resources. The daily reproductive output is substantial for a fish of this body size and underscores the species' reliance on high fecundity to offset the considerable mortality experienced during the extended larval phase.

The early life stages of Ctenochaetus binotatus begin with the release of fertilized pelagic eggs, each possessing a diameter of approximately 0.75 millimeters, a size typical for chaetodontid and acanthurid eggs. From this egg diameter, the wet weight at birth has been calculated to be approximately 0.00023 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00023 grams], a mass representative of the tiny yolk-dependent embryos that drift within the plankton. Following a brief incubation period, hatching occurs, and the prolarvae emerge as lecithotrophic larvae that rely on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac larva stage is brief, and the shift to active feeding marks a critical period of high mortality. After completing the pelagic larval phase, which may last several weeks, postflexion larvae undergo larval metamorphosis and settle onto the reef as recently metamorphosed juveniles. The initial wet weight at birth of 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams] contrasts sharply with the body mass of settled recruits, reflecting the rapid growth and tissue accumulation that occur during the planktonic feeding stage. This tiny birth mass represents the smallest body size in the species' ontogeny and sets the starting point for all subsequent somatic growth.

The maximum longevity of Ctenochaetus binotatus in its natural habitat is estimated at 20 years [am = 20 years], based on extrapolations from growth ring analysis and population size structure data collected at a stable water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. This positions the species among the longer-lived acanthurids of its size class, possibly linked to the stable food supply of algal turfs. Over the course of this 20-year maximum lifespan (20 years) [am = 20 years], individuals gradually approach their ultimate body mass, which has been estimated at 286 grams [Wwi = 286 grams] based on the species' length-weight conversion parameters at a temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. This asymptotic adult mass (286 grams) [Wwi = 286 grams] is attained only after many years of continuous feeding on the fine algal turfs that constitute the primary dietary resource. The combination of a protracted lifespan and moderate asymptotic mass suggests a life-history strategy characterized by relatively slow somatic growth rates and a delayed peak in reproductive output, a pattern typical of fish inhabiting stable, resource-limited coral reef ecosystems where adult survival is prioritized over rapid maturation.
